title: Acid–Base Properties of Monomethylgermanium(IV) in Aqueous Solutions
abstract: Abstract Monomethylgermanium (MMGe), the dominant organogermanium species in aquatic systems, exists predominantly as the neutral mononuclear species (CH 3 )Ge(OH) 3  under environmentally relevant conditions. MMGe displays conservative behavior in freshwater and marine environments, an observation consistent with high chemical stability, yet its fundamental acid–base properties remain poorly characterized. To address this gap, we investigated the protolytic properties of (CH 3 )Ge(OH) 3  at 298.2(2) K across a range of ionic strengths (0.1–1.0 mol·L −1 ) and five supporting electrolytes (LiCl, NaCl, KCl, CsCl, TMACl) by glass-electrode potentiometry. The first deprotonation constant (p K a  = –log  K 1 ) of (CH 3 )Ge(OH) 3  was consistently determined across experimental conditions with values ranging from 11.07(4) to 11.22(3), except in 1 mol·L −1  TMACl, where an anomalously high value (11.62(5)) was attributed to specific ion effects.  1 H and  13 C NMR titrations in 1 mol·L −1  KCl confirmed a single protonation equilibrium with p K a  = 11.22(1), in excellent agreement with the potentiometric results. No evidence was found for the formation of a doubly deprotonated species under the investigated p[H] range (< 13). These findings contribute fundamental thermodynamic data for MMGe and enhance our understanding of its chemical behavior in natural waters.

sections.heading: Introduction
paragraphs: Three germanium species have been identified in the natural environment: inorganic germanium (iGe), monomethylgermanium (MMGe), and dimethylgermanium (DMGe) [ 1 ]. In aquatic systems such as lakes, estuaries, and oceans, iGe exhibits nutrient-like behavior that closely mirrors that of silicon. In contrast, organogermanium species do not participate in the dynamic biogeochemical cycle typically observed for organometallic species of other metalloids (e.g., arsenic, antimony, selenium). MMGe and DMGe display conservative behavior in lakes, estuarine, and marine environments, an observation consistent with their high chemical stability in both freshwater and saline systems. Together, MMGe and DMGe account for more than 50% of detectable germanium in seawater (≈ 320 pmol·L −1  as compared to ≈ 100 pmol·L −1  iGe) and are homogeneously distributed throughout the global ocean [ 1 ]. Although continental sources are presumed to be the main origin, the contribution of ocean hydrothermal inputs cannot be completely ruled out. Based on estimates of fluvial fluxes, Lewis and Mayer [ 2 ] estimated the oceanic residence times of MMGe and DMGe from several hundred thousand to a few million years.

In organogermanium compounds, the central germanium atom is tetravalent, with a coordination number of four. These molecules feature two main types of bonds: the relatively nonpolar and inert germanium–carbon (Ge–C) bonds, and the more polar and labile germanium–ligand (Ge–L) bonds, the latter often involving donor atoms such as oxygen. Germanium compounds dissolve in water as their hydroxides ((CH 3 ) n Ge(OH) 4– n  with  n  = 0–3) over a wide pH range [ 3 ], although their acid–base properties still remain poorly understood [ 4 ].

Given MMGe’s environmental persistence and inferred chemical stability, a quantitative understanding of its acid–base behavior is essential for predicting its speciation, mobility, and potential reactivity in natural waters. The aim of this study was to investigate the protolytic properties of (CH 3 )Ge(OH) 3  in the presence of various supporting electrolytes and ionic strengths. Due to the inherent challenges associated with solution equilibrium studies in alkaline media, where protolysis is expected to occur, two complementary analytical methodologies, glass-electrode potentiometry and Nuclear Magnetic Resonance (NMR) spectroscopy, were employed to determine the corresponding apparent equilibrium constant. For practical reasons, the NMR investigation was limited to 1 mol·L −1  KCl as the background electrolyte, whereas potentiometric titrations were also performed at lower concentrations and for a selection of background electrolytes (alkali metal chlorides and tetramethylammonium chloride) at different concentrations ranging from 0.1 to 1.0 mol·L −1 .

Regarding the use of NMR,  73 Ge NMR spectroscopy would have been ideal for studying the hydrolysis of Ge(IV) derivatives, but no attempt was made here to exploit this nucleus due to two major drawbacks. The first is the low sensitivity of the  73 Ge isotope (1.4 × 10 −3  relative to the proton), resulting from both its relatively low natural abundance (7.73%) and its gyromagnetic ratio (–9.33 × 10 −8  rad·s −1 ·T −1 ) [ 5 ]. The second limitation arises from the nuclear spin of  73 Ge, which is equal to 9/2, and therefore from its relatively high quadrupole moment (–19.6 × 10 −30  m 2 ), which causes line broadening detrimental for the detection of non-symmetric species. As a result, the acid–base properties of (CH 3 )Ge(OH) 3  were studied exclusively by  1 H and  13 C NMR spectroscopy at 298.0(5) K.

sections.heading: Potentiometric Titrations
paragraphs: All solutions were prepared with water produced by a reverse osmosis unit (TGA, Genpure, Germany) without further treatment. Argon used for degassing solutions had a purity higher than 99.999 atom% and was purchased from Air Liquide, Belgium. NaCl and KCl were of analytical grade (ACS) from Roth, Germany, while tetramethylammonium chloride (TMACl) from Thermo Scientific, Germany, had a purity of more than 98%. LiCl and CsCl were from that same manufacturer and both had a purity of more than 99%. Titrations in alkali metal chloride solutions were performed with the corresponding alkali hydroxide. Standard solutions of 0.1 mol·L −1  NaOH and 0.1 mol·L −1  KOH were prepared from commercially available ampoules (Merck and Roth, respectively), LiOH from solid LiOH (98%, Thermo Scientific), and CsOH (50% solution, sealed ampoule under inert gas, Thermo Scientific). The tetramethylammonium hydroxide (TMAOH) solution was prepared from the commercially available pentahydrate salt (> 99%, Thermo Scientific, Germany), as commercial TMAOH solutions are prone to contamination by CO 2 . The absence of carbonate contamination of the standard base solutions was checked by Gran titrations [ 6 ,  7 ]. Background electrolyte solutions were checked for acidic or basic impurities by Gran titrations with very dilute bases or acids, respectively [ 8 ]. Aliquots of (CH 3 )GeCl 3  (typically 40–70 μL for each titration) were measured and handled with an adjustable micropipette (Pipetman, Gilson, France).

Initially, 100.0 mL of background electrolyte was placed in a thermoregulated (298.2(2) K) double-jacketed titration vessel and degassed by sparging with Ar. An approximately 5 mmol·L −1  (CH 3 )Ge(OH) 3  concentration was achieved by addition of about 60 µL (CH 3 )GeCl 3  (97% purity,  ρ  = 1.706 g·cm −3 , Thermo Fisher), which instantly hydrolyses to (CH 3 )Ge(OH) 3  under these conditions. The precise amount taken was determined by weighing the stock bottle, as it was found that owing to the high density of this reagent, volumes taken by a pipette that had previously been calibrated with water were inaccurate. A purity of 97% (given by the manufacturer and checked by gravimetric chloride determination of hydrolyzed aliquots) served as the basis in our calculations. The pH was brought to about 3 by the addition of 1 mL of standard base (1 mol·L −1 ) and the titration was initiated by adding 0.25 mol·L −1  standardized base from a digital burette (Brand Titrette ® , Germany) up to a final pH of about 12 (13 for titrations carried out in 1 mol·L −1  TMACl solution, as the p K a  turned out to be particularly high in this electrolyte). Typically, about 110 data points were collected for each experimental run.

The pH was measured with a digital pH meter (Mettler-Toledo SevenCompact, Switzerland) in conjunction with a combined glass electrode (SI-Analytics, Xylem, Germany or WTW, Germany). Two such electrodes were used  alternatim.  However, an Aldrich (single) glass pH electrode (Sigma–Aldrich, US), combined with a Thermo Scientific (US) Ag/AgCl double-junction reference electrode was used in the 1 mol·L −1  LiCl solution, as the alkaline error of the combined glass electrodes was so high that no meaningful measurements could be made in that particular background electrolyte. After calibration, electrodes were used for 1–2 days only and then returned to their storage solution and left to stand for at least a week.

The parameters  k i  were obtained by nonlinear regression of the potentials measured during the calibration with respect to the calculated [H]. Because of the alkali error, care was taken to extend the calibration range well into the basic domain (p[H] > 12) and beyond the highest p[H] expected in subsequent titrations. Full details of the calibration and titration procedures have been published previously [ 9 ,  10 ] and are equivalent to those detailed in the following section. The water self-dissociation constant ( K w ) was treated as a constant in the electrode calibration function. The corresponding values for the various electrolyte solutions and ionic strengths considered in this work are summarized in Table  1  and were calculated using the Specific Ion interaction Theory (SIT) model with data from Brown and Ekberg [ 11 ]. Densities of the electrolyte solutions were taken from Söhnel and Novotny [ 12 ]. In the case of TMACl,  K w  values were taken from Sipos et al. [ 13 ]. Because of frequent electrode calibrations, titration replicates were not all obtained on the same day, but typically within 24 h of calibration.

sections.heading: NMR Titrations
paragraphs: Double-deionized ultra-pure water (18.2 MΩ cm) was obtained from a PURELAB ®  Chorus I Analytical (Elga) cartridge system. KCl (ACS reagent > 99%, Sigma-Aldrich) was used as received. Analytical grade KOH pellets (SDS) were thoroughly washed with water to eliminate the potassium carbonate crust and wiped with KimTech TM  paper (Kimberly-Clark) prior to dissolution in ultra-pure water. The concentration of the resulting stock solution ( c  = 0.871 mol·L −1 ) was determined by volumetric titration against a standardized 0.1 mol·L −1  HCl solution (Titrisol ® , Merck) delivered by a Titrando 904 (Metrohm) automatic titration setup equipped with a 5 mL piston burette (more details about the equipment can be found in the Supporting Information). Two KOH working solutions of 0.2 and 0.5 mol·L −1  were prepared by dilution with ultra-pure water and their ionic strength adjusted to 1 mol·L −1  by dissolving the required amount of solid KCl.

In a first run, 17 NMR samples of 500 µL each were prepared the same day in small vials by mixing 75 µL of the acidic (CH 3 )Ge(OH) 3  mother solution ([Ge] = 0.03978 mol·L −1 , [HCl] = 0.1193 mol·L −1 ), 25 µL of D 2 O (99.90% D, Eurisotop), 5 µL of dioxane for chemical shift calibration purposes,  x  µL of the aqueous 0.2 or 0.5 mol·L −1  KOH working solution,  y  µL of an aqueous 3 mol·L −1  KCl solution to adjust the final ionic strength to  I  = 1 mol·L −1 , and (395 −  x  −  y ) µL of ultra-pure water. Accordingly, the final germanium concentration was 5.97 mmol·L −1 , that of potassium ranged between 0.99 and 1.01 mol·L −1 , while the chloride concentration varied between 0.96 and 0.99 mol·L −1 . After p[H] and NMR measurements, the most basic samples 12–17 were combined three days after their initial preparation and 5 new solutions were obtained by adding various amounts of 0.871 mol·L −1  KOH to 500 µL aliquots of the mixture, allowing to reach p[H] values ranging from 12.10 to 13.03, while the total germanium, potassium, and chloride concentrations for sample 22 dropped to 4.59 mmol·L −1 , 0.978 mol·L −1 , and 0.751 mol·L −1 , respectively. The exact composition of each NMR sample can be found in Table S1. Since both sets of solutions were prepared at different days, the glass electrode was freshly calibrated before measuring the p[H] of each series. Prior to each single measurement, the corresponding vial was immersed for 5 min in a closed water bath maintained at 298.2(2) K by a Lauda RE106 circulator, while being kept under an argon atmosphere to avoid CO 2  uptake from air by the test solution.

The p[H] of each solution was measured with a PHM 240 ionometer (Radiometer) fitted with a combined semi-micro high-alkalinity glass electrode (ref. 6.0234.110, Metrohm). The Ag/AgCl reference compartment was filled with a saturated AgCl/KCl solution. As for potentiometric titrations, the electrode was calibrated as a hydronium ion concentration probe for an ionic strength of  I  = 1 mol·L −1  over a p[H] range spanning from 1 to 12.8 by performing HCl/KOH titrations. Considering the low amount of D 2 O (5%) added for locking the spectrometer frequency, no corrections for the isotopic effect has been applied as the expected contribution (less than + 0.02 p[H] unit as compared to pure H 2 O [ 14 ]) remains within experimental error. Further details can be found in the Supporting Information.

The  1 H and  13 C NMR spectra of all 22 samples were recorded on a Bruker Avance III HD spectrometer operating at 600.33 MHz, equipped with a 5 mm BBOF Prodigy cryoprobe and an SampleCase™ automatic sample changer with 24 positions. Spectra were acquired at 298.0(5) K using the TopSpin™ 3.6.1 software.  1 H NMR spectra were recorded using the zg30 pulse sequence with a relaxation delay ( d 1) of 1 s, a spectral width ( SW ) of 20 ppm, 65,000 points in the time domain ( TD ), and 16 scans ( NS ).  13 C NMR spectra were recorded using the zgpg30 pulse sequence with  d 1 = 2 s,  SW  = 240 ppm,  TD  = 65,000, and  NS  = 2048. Chemical shifts ( δ ) are reported in parts per million (ppm) relative to tetramethylsilane. Spectra were calibrated with respect to dioxane:  δ H  = 3.75 ppm,  δ C  = 67.19 ppm [ 15 ].

NMR data processing was carried out by unweighted nonlinear least squares refinements with the OriginPro 2018 package. For each refined parameter, the standard deviation ( σ ) returned by the minimization routine is reported in parentheses.

sections.heading: Potentiometry
paragraphs: In dilute aqueous solutions, MMGe is known to exist predominantly as the neutral mononuclear species (CH 3 )Ge(OH) 3  [ 3 ], which undergoes protolysis under alkaline conditions. Its acid–base properties were investigated at 298.2(1) K by glass-electrode potentiometry in five different chloride media, using LiCl, NaCl, KCl, CsCl, and TMACl as supporting electrolytes. For each salt, the ionic strength was set to 0.1 and 1.0 mol· L −1 . In the case of NaCl, additional measurements were performed at  I  = 0.15 and 0.67 mol·L −1 , corresponding to near physiological and seawater salinities.

At least three titration curves for each electrolyte system were used to simultaneously calculate the first apparent p K a  values (p K a  = –log  K 1 , Eq. ( 3 )) of (CH 3 )Ge(OH) 3  by using the proprietary software ReactLab pH Pro (Jplus Consulting Ltd., Australia). The program minimizes the residual square sum between the experimental and predicted titration curves by iterative refinement of the free model parameters (the variables) using a modified Marquardt–Levenberg algorithm. In addition to the residual square sum, the standard deviation of each refined parameter and the overall residual standard deviation are provided at the end of the iteration process. The free parameters were calculated  in the concentration domain , with the software’s automatic conversion to activities disabled. During refinement, the initial proton concentration was also treated as a variable; its simultaneous optimization considerably improved the overall fit. This adjustment was necessary because the germanium species under investigation was generated in situ by hydrolysis of the trichloride, leading to the concomitant formation of HCl. Despite its high aqueous solubility, some gaseous HCl inevitably escaped, resulting in uncertainty in the initial total proton concentration, while the concentration of the (non-volatile) germanium species remained reliably known. Conversely, the autoprotolysis constant of water ( K w , Table  1 ) was treated as a fixed parameter throughout the refinement process.

The mean p K a  values under the various experimental conditions are summarized in Table  2 , along with the standard deviation  σ n –1  computed for  n  replicates. Notably, all attempts to include the doubly deprotonated [(CH 3 )Ge(OH)O 2 ] 2−  species in the chemical model failed to improve the fit quality, indicating that it does not form in appreciable amounts over the entire p[H] range explored (p[H] < 12). Likewise, data fitting provided no evidence for the formation of partially deprotonated polynuclear Ge(IV) species at the investigated concentration level ( ca . 4 mmol·L −1 ), in agreement with earlier reports [ 16 ].
 Table 2 Values of the p K a  of (CH 3 )Ge(OH) 3  and their standard deviations ( σ n –1 ) for  n  replicates determined by glass-electrode potentiometry in various electrolyte systems at different ionic strengths Electrolyte Concentration/mol·L −1 p K a  ±  σ n –1 n LiCl 0.1 11.21 ± 0.03 3 LiCl 1.0 11.14 ± 0.10 3 NaCl 0.1 11.16 ± 0.03 3 NaCl 0.15 11.16 ± 0.03 3 NaCl 0.67 11.07 ± 0.04 3 NaCl 1.0 11.08 ± 0.03 3 KCl 0.1 11.22 ± 0.03 5 KCl 1.0 11.17 ± 0.05 7 CsCl 0.1 11.10 ± 0.03 4 CsCl 1.0 11.16 ± 0.03 3 TMACl 0.1 11.17 ± 0.04 3 TMACl 1.0 11.62 ± 0.05 3 T  = 298.2(2) K

It was also experimentally confirmed that after titrating the initially acidic solution with standardized base, a closely matching titration curve was obtained upon subsequent titration of the basic solution with standardized acid. The absence of hysteresis demonstrated that each point along the experimental curve represents a true equilibrium state, further confirming that the determination of the protolysis constants  K 1  was not influenced by kinetic effects or the formation of a precipitate.

Figure  1 b displays a distribution diagram computed under typical titration conditions ( c Ge  = 4 mmol·L −1 ) in 0.1 mol·L −1  KCl using the average value of p K a  = 11.22 reported in Table  2 . Accordingly, (CH 3 )Ge(OH) 3  is the only stable form of MMGe up to p[H] = 9, while at the end-points of the titrations close to p[H] 12, the deprotonated species [(CH 3 )Ge(OH) 2 O] −  represents nearly 80% of the total amount of germanium.

sections.heading: NMR Spectroscopy
paragraphs: As a higher total germanium concentration had to be used as compared to potentiometry, NMR titrations as a function of p[H] were conducted only for an ionic strength of  I  = 1 mol·L −1  adjusted by adding the adequate amount of KCl. Stack-plots of spectra are reproduced in Figs. S1 and S2, respectively. The chemical shift variation of the methyl signal was monitored over a wide p[H] range (1.74–13.03) in the H 2 O/D 2 O 95:5 v/v mixture without precipitation (Fig.  2 ). At p[H] values lower than 8, the methyl protons and carbon atom of (CH 3 )Ge(OH) 3  resonate as singlets at 0.84 and –0.76 ppm, respectively. Upon raising the p[H] above 8, the proton signal moves progressively to higher fields, while the carbon signal shifts in the opposite direction until a plateau is reached around p[H] ≈ 13. Fig. 2 1 H (squares) and  13 C (circles) NMR titration as a function of p[H] of (CH 3 )Ge(OH) 3  ( c Ge  = 4.59–5.97 mol·L −1 ) with KOH using a 600 MHz spectrometer. Apparent chemical shifts ( δ obs ) are plotted as a function of p[H] measured by a high-alkalinity glass electrode. The five most basic data points (18–22) were collected three days after the others after mixing samples 12–17 and readjusting the p[H] of the solutions with 0.871 mol·L −1  KOH (see Table S1 for further details). Lines correspond to the best-fit curves using Eq. ( 7 ). Solvent: H 2 O/D 2 O 95/5 v/v,  I  = 1 mol·L −1  K(Cl/OH),  T  = 298.0(5) K

To improve the matrix conditioning, the right-side expression of Eq. ( 7 ) was used to analyze simultaneously by unweighted nonlinear least squares the  1 H and  13 C chemical shift variations as a function of p[H]. The values of the five refined parameters are p K a  = 11.22(1),  δ H 10  = 0.835(2),  δ H 1–1  = 0.564(3),  δ C 10  = –0.755(2), and  δ C 1–1  = 0.200(4) ppm. The corresponding best-fit curves shown in Fig.  2  as solid lines are overlaid to the experimental data points. The almost perfect match ( σ  = 0.008 ppm for 38 degrees of freedom) further confirms that a single proton exchange equilibrium (Eq. ( 2 )) occurs between p[H] 9.5 and 13.0. A posteriori speciation calculation with log  K 1  = 11.22 confirmed that the total ionic strength for all 22 data points remained nearly constant (0.976 ≤  I  ≤ 1.004 mol·L −1 ), the largest deviations occurring for the three most basic solutions (p[H] > 12.7). Most gratifyingly, the p K a  value derived from the single NMR titration experiment (11.22(1)) is in very good agreement with the mean value obtained by potentiometry (11.17(5)) for 7 replicates in 1 mol·L −1  KCl.

sections.heading: Discussion
paragraphs: Considering the experimental standard deviations and the errors associated with potentiometric measurements in highly alkaline media, the mean p K a  values reported in Table  2  for all five supporting electrolytes are generally consistent, with one exception. Specifically, the value for 1 mol·L −1  TMACl (11.62(5)) clearly stands out as an outlier, as the four other values obtained at the same ionic strength for the alkali metal chlorides (MCl) fall within a narrow range spanning 11.08(3) for Na +  to 11.17(5) for K +  with an average of 11.14(4). The exact cause of this discrepancy remains unclear, but significant deviations from ideal electrolyte solution behavior are frequently observed in concentrated tetraalkylammonium salt solutions. These deviations are attributed to solvation effects, the large hydrodynamic radius, and the tetrahedral geometry of the lipophilic NR 4 +  cations. However, the protolysis constant in 0.1 mol·L −1  TMACl (11.17(4)) is not significantly different from those determined in LiCl (11.21(3)), NaCl (11.16(3)), and KCl (11.22(3)), with an average of 11.19(3) across these four media. In contrast, the value for 0.1 mol·L −1  CsCl (11.10(3)) appears slightly lower. This deviation most likely reflects experimental error rather than a genuine chemical “cesium effect”, especially since the value found in 1 mol·L −1  CsCl (11.16(3)) aligns well with those found for the other alkali metal containing media. Overall, the reported data at both ionic strengths show no clear dependency of p K a  on the atomic number of the M +  cation, allowing for the safe exclusion of ion-pair formation between [(CH 3 )Ge(OH) 2 O] −  and the counterion of the supporting electrolyte.

Since the p K a  was measured at 298.2(2) K for four different ionic strengths in NaCl ( I  = 0.1, 0.15, 0.67, and 1.0 mol·L −1 ), this series of data was used to estimate the p K a 0  value at infinite dilution by the SIT method after converting the conditional p K a ’s from the molar into the molal (p K a m ) concentration scale. Calculation details and definitions of all parameters can be found in [ 17 ] and in any volume of the  Chemical Thermodynamics Series  published by the OECD Nuclear Energy Agency Thermochemical Data Base Project (NEA-TDB:  https://www.oecd-nea.org/jcms/pl_22166/thermochemical-database-tdb-project ). The weighted linear regression [ 18 ] for the four data points reported in Table  2  for NaCl solutions leads to p K a 0  (298.15 K) = 11.379 ± 0.048 and Δ ε  = (0.098 ± 0.080) kg·mol −1  (Fig.  3 ), with Δ ε  =  ε ((CH 3 )Ge(OH) 3 ,NaCl) −  ε (Na + ,[(CH 3 )Ge(OH) 2 O] − ) −  ε (H + ,Cl − ), at the 95% probability level. Parametrization of Eq. S5 (see Supporting Information) allows the reliable estimation of the conditional protolysis constant in NaCl at any ionic strength lower than 1 mol·L −1 . Fig. 3 SIT plot for the protolysis reaction of (CH 3 )Ge(OH) 3  based on the data given in Table  2 . Black dots, NaCl data. The solid line results from the weighted linear regression of these data, where the slope corresponds to the SIT interaction coefficient Δ ε , and the y-axis intercept to the stability constant at zero ionic strength (p K a 0 , 298.15 K). The dotted lines represent the 95% associated uncertainty range extrapolated from zero to higher ionic strengths. Symbols: red, LiCl; blue, KCl; brown, KCl (NMR spectroscopy); green, CsCl

The set of p K a m  values determined in the other supporting electrolytes have also been included in Fig.  3 , but for comparison purposes only, as no attempts to refine each specific Δ ε  parameter was undertaken because of the limited number of ionic strengths investigated. Considering the confidence intervals at 95% probability estimated for the values in NaCl, the corresponding SIT parameters can be applied in first approximation but with good confidence for estimating the p K a m  values in LiCl, KCl, and CsCl solutions at least up to  I m  = 1 kg·mol −1 . However, values in TMACl were not included in Fig.  3  as the activity coefficients in tetraalkylammonium halide solutions cannot be accurately estimated by the SIT model, among others because the specific ion interaction coefficients  ε (R 4 N + ,X − ) depend on the ionic strength [ 17 ].

A second approach to p K a 0  estimation was based on the simultaneous analysis of the p K a ’s determined for all alkaline chloride salts using the JESS software ( http://jess.murdoch.edu.au ) based on the equation proposed by May [ 19 ]. Figure  4  shows the predicted variation of p K a  with ionic strength. The value obtained for p K a 0  is 11.38(1). The result looks reasonable. Fig. 4 Variation of the p K a  values of (CH 3 )Ge(OH) 3  determined by potentiometry in the different electrolyte solutions as a function of the molar ionic strength ( I ) as calculated by JESS. The line corresponds to the predicted variation of p K a . Symbols: red, LiCl; black, NaCl; blue, KCl; brown, KCl (NMR spectroscopy); green, CsCl; magenta, Me 4 NCl

As compared to Ge(OH) 4  (p K a 0  = 9.10 [ 16 ]), MMGe behaves as a much weaker acid. The more than two orders of magnitude higher p K a 0  value found for the latter is a direct consequence of the inductive electron-donating effect of the methyl group, which increases the electron density on the Ge(IV) center and, consequently, enhances the basicity of the [(CH 3 )Ge(OH) 2 O] −  anion. Conversely, the latter conjugated base accepts more readily a proton than its non-methylated and less basic [Ge(OH) 3 O] −  counterpart. A second p K a 0  value of 12.76 has been selected for Ge(OH) 4  by Filella and May in their critical review [ 16 ]. Accordingly, the second deprotonation of MMGe could be expected to occur only in very strongly alkaline solutions ([OH − ] ≫ 0.1 mol·L −1 ), which explains why the formation of [(CH 3 )Ge(OH)O 2 ] 2−  remained undetectable by NMR spectroscopy up to p[H] 13. Following the same reasoning and assuming an increase of the first protolysis constant with the number of bound electro-donating methyl groups, the p K a  values of (CH 3 ) 2 Ge(OH) 2  (DMGe) is also expected to exceed 13. Nevertheless, the anticipated basicity increase based on pure electronic effects might be partially mitigated by the higher lipophilicity of the dimethyl derivative.

sections.heading: Conclusion
paragraphs: Investigations of the acid–base properties of MMGe in five different alkaline media by combining glass-electrode potentiometry with  1 H and  13 C NMR titrations enabled us to ascertain the exclusive formation of the singly deprotonated [(CH 3 )Ge(OH) 2 O] −  species over a wide p[H] range (9–13). Reliable and consistent p K a  values were obtained by numerical analysis of the potentiometric and spectroscopic data sets. Titrations performed with NaCl as supporting electrolyte at four different concentrations covering the 0.1–1 mol·L −1  range allowed to derive the yet unavailable thermodynamic protolysis constant (p K a 0  = 11.38(5) at 95% probability level) and to parametrize two simple equations describing the ionic strength dependence of p K a  values at 25.0 °C. The chosen models are the Specific Ion interaction Theory and a variant of the Guggenheim equation proposed by May [ 19 ]. Equilibrium data acquired in other alkaline salt solutions (LiCl, KCl, and CsCl) at  I  = 0.1 and 1 mol·L −1  are, within experimental error, in good agreement with those determined in NaCl, suggesting that both equations can also be applied to these media. It is noteworthy that we found no evidence for ion-pairing of [(CH 3 )Ge(OH) 2 O] −  with the alkaline cation of the background electrolyte. Nevertheless, the p K a  value measured in 1 mol·L −1  tetramethylammonium chloride deviates significantly from those obtained for the other salts at the same ionic strength. Owing to the inductive donor effect of the methyl substituent, MMGe is two orders of magnitude more basic than the inorganic form of Ge(IV), Ge(OH) 4 . While the latter undergoes a second protolysis with a p K a 0  of 12.6, our experimental study clearly ruled out that process for MMGe, suggesting that it might occur at base concentrations well above 0.1 mol·L −1 . Altogether, the solution equilibrium constants derived herein provide a solid basis for modeling the distribution of MMGe species, contributing thereby to a better understanding of the fate of organic germanium in environmental matrices where MMGe occurs exclusively as the neutral species (CH₃)Ge(OH)₃. Its neutral character may help explain its chemical inertness and, consequently, its conservative behavior in natural systems.
